title: Cognitive-affective functions, neighborhood opportunity, and social functioning in youth with neurofibromatosis type 1
abstract: Abstract Objective This study evaluated associations between social functioning and cognitive-affective functions (CAF), including executive function, face processing, and theory of mind, and neighborhood opportunity, in youth with neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1). Methods Youth with NF1 (n = 37), ages 8–14 (M = 11.8 years), with no prior autism diagnosis, completed assessments of CAF and peer relationships. Parents completed questionnaires on executive function skills, social impairments, and peer relationships. The Childhood Opportunity Index national composite score quantified neighborhood opportunity. Correlation and hierarchical linear regression analyses evaluated associations between social functioning, CAF, and neighborhood opportunity. Results Executive functioning and neighborhood opportunity were significantly associated with parent reports of social impairments and peer relationships. Executive functioning and facial expression recognition were correlated with self-reported peer relationships, but were not significant in regression models. Facial identity recognition was significantly correlated with social impairments and parent-rated peer relationships. Theory of mind was not associated with any outcome. Conclusions Findings underscore the interplay between CAF, neighborhood opportunity, and social functioning in children with NF1. Case conceptualizations should integrate social determinants of health with measures of cognition and behavior. Longitudinal research is needed to understand mechanisms driving variability in social outcomes and inform equitable care.
